item.title: “Deep, Ānanda, is this dependent origination, and deep indeed is its definition. It is because of not understanding, not penetrating this Dhamma, Ānanda, that beings…
item.description:
“Deep, Ānanda, is this dependent origination, and deep indeed is its definition. It is because of not understanding, not penetrating this Dhamma, Ānanda, that beings are tangled like a ball of thread, covered with blight, like muñja grass, like bulrushes, unable to escape from the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower realm, saṃsāra. Ānanda, one who dwells seeing gratification in things that are clung to — craving increases. With craving as condition, existence comes to be. With existence as condition, birth comes to be. With birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Such is the origination of this whole mass of suffering. Just as, Ānanda, a great tree, having its roots that extend downward and laterally, all those roots convey the sap upwards — that great tree, being nourished and sustained in such a way, would stand for a long time. So too, Ānanda, one who dwells seeing gratification in things that are clung to — craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging comes to be … Such is the origination of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.60

item.title: “Rādha, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near — all form should…
item.description:
“Rādha, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near — all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling … perception … formations … consciousness there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near — all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Rādha, knowing thus, seeing thus, regarding this conscious body and all external signs, there is no ‘I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.71

item.title: “And what, Ānanda, is the perception of peril? Here, Ānanda, a monk, going to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an…
item.description:
“And what, Ānanda, is the perception of peril? Here, Ānanda, a monk, going to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects: ‘This body is of much suffering, of much peril. Various diseases arise in this body, such as: eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-edge disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, aging, abdominal pain, fainting, dysentery, colic, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, tuberculosis, epilepsy, skin disease, itch, scab, ringworm, scabies, blood-bile disorder, diabetes, hemorrhoids, cancer, sores, ulcerations; diseases born of bile, born of phlegm, born of wind, born of the combination of humors; diseases born of change of season, born of improper behavior, born of sudden assault, born of the result of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination.’ Thus he dwells contemplating peril in this body.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.60
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these two kinds of search: the noble search and the ignoble search. And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, a…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these two kinds of search: the noble search and the ignoble search. And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to birth seeks what is also subject to birth; being himself subject to aging seeks what is subject to aging; being subject to sickness … subject to death … subject to sorrow … subject to defilement seeks what is subject to defilement. And what, monks, do you call ‘subject to birth’? Wife and children are subject to birth; male and female slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; fowl and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth. Monks, these attachments are subject to birth, and he, being himself subject to birth, being tied to them, infatuated, and utterly committed to them, seeks what is subject to birth.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta

item.title: “Monks, how is it that Māra and his followers cannot reach? Here, monks, a monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states,…
item.description:
“Monks, how is it that Māra and his followers cannot reach? Here, monks, a monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, obliterated Māra’s track, leaving no trace, making Māra unable to find his path. Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the stilling of initial and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, without initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called a monk who has blinded Māra, obliterated Māra’s track, leaving no trace, making Māra unable to find his path.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 25 – Nivāpasutta

item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that leads to such great harm as heedlessness. Heedlessness, monks, leads to great harm.”
item.description:

item.title: The foolish, ignorant person delights in heedlessness, But the wise one guards heedlessness as his greatest treasure. Do not yield to heedlessness, do not yield…
item.description:
The foolish, ignorant person delights in heedlessness,
But the wise one guards heedlessness as his greatest treasure.
Do not yield to heedlessness, do not yield to sensual pleasures.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 86 – Aṅgulimālasutta

item.title: “Monks, evil, unwholesome states arise with a sign, not without a sign. By abandoning that sign, those evil, unwholesome states are not present. Monks, evil,…
item.description:
“Monks, evil, unwholesome states arise with a sign, not without a sign. By abandoning that sign, those evil, unwholesome states are not present. Monks, evil, unwholesome states arise with a cause, not without a cause. By abandoning that cause, those evil, unwholesome states are not present. Monks, evil, unwholesome states arise with a form, not without a form … arise with a feeling … with a perception … with consciousness, not without consciousness. By abandoning that cause, those evil, unwholesome states are not present.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.77
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “So too, monks, a monk reflecting thus gains great benefit in wholesome states. ‘Do I dwell much with greed? Do I dwell much without greed?…
item.description:
“So too, monks, a monk reflecting thus gains great benefit in wholesome states. ‘Do I dwell much with greed? Do I dwell much without greed? Do I dwell much with a mind of ill-will? Do I dwell much with a mind without ill-will? Do I dwell much overcome by sloth and torpor, or do I dwell much with sloth and torpor abandoned? Do I dwell much with restlessness, or do I dwell much without restlessness? Do I dwell much with doubt, or do I dwell much with doubt overcome? Do I dwell much with anger, or do I dwell much without anger? Do I dwell much with a defiled mind, or do I dwell much with an undefiled mind? Do I dwell much with bodily fever, or do I dwell much without bodily fever? Do I dwell much with laziness, or do I dwell much with energy and striving? Do I dwell much unconcentrated, or do I dwell much concentrated?’”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.51
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And, Carpenter, what is the practice that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome thoughts? Here, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his…
item.description:
“And, Carpenter, what is the practice that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome thoughts? Here, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives so that unarisen evil, unwholesome states do not arise … so that arisen evil, unwholesome states are abandoned … so that unarisen wholesome states arise … so that arisen wholesome states are maintained, not confused, increased, expanded, developed, and fulfilled. Such is the practice that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome thoughts.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 78 – Samaṇamuṇḍikasutta
